strengths: The paper addresses a natural and clearly motivated question: can the redundant forward dynamics model in latent action model (LAM) training be replaced by the pretrained video-generation world model itself? The framing and related work position this well against two-stage pipelines (Genie, AdaWorld, Motus, DWS).

The empirical study of joint-training collapse (Figure 2) is informative: the codebook utilization/entropy diagnostics, the test with a randomly initialized world model, and the warm-up length sweep (Figure 3) provide a plausible mechanistic account of why naive joint training fails and how warm-up mitigates it.

The controlled ablations in Section 4.3 (pure warm-up vs. E2E, frozen LAM vs. evolving LAM) directly probe the claimed 'co-evolution' mechanism from both directions, and Appendix D.1 offers quantitative codebook evidence for the downstream adaptation fragility of the two-stage baseline.

The evaluation spans multiple datasets (OXE, EgoCentric, AgiBot, LIBERO), a second video-generation backbone (Wan2.1, Appendix D.4), scalability analyses (model size, batch size), and a downstream planning benchmark (VP^2), with a transparent compute-cost comparison (Table 8).
weaknesses: The core contribution is a fairly narrow training recipe: replacing the FDM with the world model plus a frozen-teacher warm-up. Notably, the proposed method is itself effectively sequential (8K steps of training the IDM against a frozen world model before joint training), which substantially blurs the claimed dichotomy between 'two-stage' and 'one-stage/joint' paradigms. The novelty over AdaWorld-style staged finetuning is incremental.

The central claim of a 'higher-quality latent action space' is not supported by the direct measurement: in Table 5, linear probing shows the two-stage LAM is better or comparable on half the datasets (RT-1, LIBERO, and roughly KUKA/DROID), and the paper concedes the gap is 'subtle.' The defense rests on downstream metrics, but this weakens the headline claim as stated.

There is an experimental asymmetry that favors the proposed method: Appendix B.3 states that random-crop augmentation is used whenever the LAM is being updated (including all joint-training phases) but not when the LAM is fixed (the world-model-training stage of the baseline). This inconsistent augmentation policy could disadvantage the 2-stage baseline, and no ablation isolates its effect.

No statistical rigor: all tables report single-run point estimates with no seeds, variance, or significance tests, despite differences between methods that are often small (e.g., PSNR gaps of ~0.3-0.5 in Table 1 and Table 2). Some conclusions (e.g., 'matches or surpasses across all datasets') rest on differences well within plausible run-to-run noise.

The planning gains (Table 3) are based on very low absolute success rates and 5 runs, and the AdaWorld comparison numbers are imported rather than re-run under identical conditions; on several tasks the proposed method also performs poorly (e.g., Push Slide at 4%).

The claimed data/compute efficiency comparisons are constructed favorably: the headline 'Warm8K + E2E30K rivals LAM30K + WM30K' compares against a specific baseline budget, while the LAM8K + WM52K baseline is admittedly 'under-trained' — an odd configuration whose inclusion mainly strengthens the narrative.
No code release is mentioned, and the curated 13-dataset human-video mixture is complex to reproduce; reproducibility relies on appendix hyperparameters alone.
